sources.title: List of Fabric Faults Created During Dyeing and Their Remedies
Preventive Measurement of Fabric Shade Variation in Dyeing
List of Checking and Control Points of Dyeing Process
Comparative Study of Cotton Fabric Quality Using Different Salts in Reactive Dyeing Process

_note: Facts and figures below are summarised in our own words from the four Textile Learner articles cited above, not copied verbatim — every entry carries a source_key back to its article. This is a curated subset (rope/jet dyeing faults, one QC framework, one salt trial), not a full mirror of the site's ~400-post dyeing category; see dyeing-engine.js's own header for why the recipe/costing layer stays separate from this advisory layer.

faults.name: Uneven Dyeing in Rope (Rope Dyeing Machines)
causes: Dyes and chemicals dosed too quickly into the bath
Inconsistent pretreatment (scouring, bleaching, de-sizing) across the same lot
Loose control of machine speed, temperature, dosing time, pump/reel speed, or liquor ratio
remedies: Dose dyes and chemicals at a steadily increasing rate rather than all at once
Standardise pretreatment across the whole lot before dyeing starts
Lock down machine speed, temperature, dosing time and M:L ratio as a fixed SOP
Recheck rope length and chamber loading calculations before starting

faults.name: Rope-to-Rope Uneven Shade
causes: Rope length differs from chamber to chamber
Fabric flow speed differs across nozzles
remedies: Keep rope length identical in every chamber of the machine
Equalise fabric flow speed at all nozzles

faults.name: Dye Spots
causes: Dyestuff not fully dissolved/mixed before addition to the bath
High bath water hardness
Insufficient bath agitation
remedies: Filter dissolved dye through a fine mesh before adding it to the bath
Use a sequestering agent to bring down bath hardness
Ensure adequate agitation throughout the run

faults.name: Shade Variation — Within and Between Batches
causes: Oversized pad / batching size on the jigger
Batching held too long before the next step
Salt added incorrectly (rate or timing)
Uneven dye liquor level or padder pressure across roller width
Worn squeeze rollers
Fabric-to-fabric variation in dye affinity within the same lot
Liquor ratio changed between batches instead of held constant
Different dyeing procedures used batch to batch (timing, temperature, chemical sequence)
Poor or inconsistent water quality (pH, hardness, sodium carbonate content)
remedies: Verify dye-affinity uniformity of the fabric lot before batching
Hold liquor ratio constant, scaled strictly by material weight
Keep nozzle-pass count identical across the batch
Standardise the procedure: same chemical timing, same temperature profile, every batch
Use the same dye/auxiliary combination for a given shade, not substitutes
Test incoming water quality daily rather than assuming it is constant

faults.name: Cockling
causes: Nozzle diameter too small
Liquor ratio too low
Fabric running too fast through the nozzle
remedies: Increase nozzle diameter
Raise the liquor ratio
Reduce fabric speed

faults.name: Crack, Rope and Running Marks
causes: Machine overloaded beyond its rated capacity
Nozzle pressure too low
Fabric run too slowly, or bath drained while still too hot
remedies: Reduce machine loading and raise nozzle pressure
Pre-set/pre-relax the fabric before dyeing
Raise fabric speed; slow the rinsing and cooling rate; watch drain temperature

faults.name: Crow's Feet / Wrinkling
causes: Rope speed too low
Liquor ratio too low
remedies: Pre-set/pre-relax the fabric before dyeing
Raise rope speed and liquor ratio

faults.name: Crush Marks
causes: Fabric speed too low
Liquor ratio too low
Cooling rate too fast
remedies: Raise fabric speed
Raise liquor ratio
Slow the cooling rate

faults.name: Elephant Skin / Orange Peel Effect
causes: Liquor ratio too low
Fabric overfed into the machine
Bath dropped at too high a temperature and refilled with cold water
remedies: Confirm the machine is not overloaded and has adequate liquor
Run a lab-scale trial before the bulk batch

faults.name: Crease Mark
causes: Cycle time too long
Faulty plaiting device
Uneven selvedge tension
Bow expander mis-set
Uneven heating/cooling rate or poor fabric movement
remedies: Apply an anti-creasing agent

faults.name: Patchy Dyeing
causes: Uneven heating across the jigger
Poor impregnation in the pad trough
Dye migration during an intermediate drying/dyeing step
remedies: Ensure the steam pipe runs the full machine width
Check the padding mangle is correctly configured

faults.name: Specky Dyeing
causes: Excess foam in the pad trough
Water droplets falling onto the fabric
Insufficient after-treatment
remedies: Use an antifoaming agent
Prevent droplet contact and condense water on the ager before it can drip
Keep guide rollers free of dye deposits
Give the fabric sufficient after-treatment

faults.name: Dark and Light Selvedges
causes: Uneven batching on the jigger
Batching held too long during vat dyeing
remedies: Correct the jigger's batch configuration
Adjust batch length for vat dyeing
Calibrate the expander roller before padding

qc_framework.title: Five-Stage Shade-Variation Prevention Checklist
qc_framework.summary: A batch-to-batch shade-consistency checklist spanning preparatory, dyeing, finishing, soaping and machinery stages — the concrete numeric targets are what turn 'be more careful' into something checkable on the floor.

checks: Batch weights match precisely across the lot
Fabric GSM recorded before and after scouring/bleaching
Water quality monitored: hardness, TDS, pH
RFD fabric checked for whiteness and absorbency
Residual alkali and peroxide levels checked
Scouring/bleaching weight loss tracked — should not vary by more than 2-3% batch to batch
Dye/chemical quality inspected before use
Salt run time standardised (e.g. a fixed 30 minutes every batch, not 'about half an hour')
Soda dosing duration held constant
Temperature rise timed the same way every batch
Bath pH logged every 30 minutes; held at 11-11.2 after soda addition
Water level in the bath kept consistent
Cold/hot wash timing and temperature standardised
Acetic acid dosed precisely, pH monitored
Softener quality held consistent batch to batch
Soaping agent quality checked
TDS kept below 100 ppm
Temperature, timing and dosage held uniform
Drying temperature kept consistent
Rope length uniform across batches
Nozzle-pass count consistent
Program/SOP standardised machine to machine
Filter kept clean; nozzle diameter fixed, not drifting with wear

process_checkpoints.title: Dyeing Floor Checking & Control Points
process_checkpoints.summary: A shift-level checklist for what a dyeing floor should verify before, during and after a batch, grouped by what's being checked.

points: Fabric receipt matches the production plan
Quantity verified in both metres and kilograms
Machine speed configured for the batch
Recipe prepared and verified before starting
Shade uniformity checked across the fabric
Shade compared against the approved standard
Water fully drained and refreshed between wash steps
Machine ID, design number, metres, kilograms, colour and chemicals used all logged
Completed batches removed and transferred promptly

control_points: Acceptance criteria for fastness and rubbing/friction values
Post-treatment choice, decided by dye type and shade depth

salt_comparison.title: Electrolyte (Salt) Choice in Reactive Dyeing — Common Salt vs Glauber Salt vs Vacuum Salt
salt_comparison.summary: A trial dyeing cotton at liquor ratio 1:10 with three electrolytes at 40/50/60 g/l each, comparing fabric handle, shade strength, and the wastewater burden each one leaves behind.

salts.name: Common Salt (NaCl)
salts.handle: Rougher fabric handle than Glauber salt

salts.name: Glauber Salt (Na2SO4.10H2O)
salts.handle: Smoother fabric handle; consistently higher shade strength than common salt at the same dosage
salts.tds_reduction_vs_baseline: Roughly 15-20% lower bath TDS than common/vacuum salt, easing the effluent-treatment load

salts.name: Vacuum Salt
salts.handle: Similar hardness impact to common salt

salt_comparison.rubbing_fastness_note: All three salts landed at roughly the same rubbing fastness (dry 4-4/5, wet 3/4-4) — salt choice barely moved this parameter, so the real trade-off is handle, shade strength and effluent load, not fastness.
salt_comparison.takeaway: Where wastewater hardness/TDS is a real constraint (ETP capacity, discharge limits), Glauber salt is the better electrolyte at an equivalent dosage — same fastness, better handle, far less hardness added.
